sentences.text: Patagornis was a small terror bird, standing about 15% larger than a modern rhea.
The animal stood approximately 0.9 to 1 meter tall at the back and weighed between 45 and 50 kilograms.
It had a tall and elongated skull similar to those of Andalgalornis and Andrewsornis, measuring between 33.7 cm and 34.5 cm in length.
The creature possessed small abdomens and wings relative to its long, lithe hindlimbs.
The skull of the most complete specimen measures 33.7 cm in length and 12 cm in width.
Fossils preserve large, spur-like quill knobs on the ulna that likely served as attachment points for long feathers.
Research from 2005 estimated Patagornis had a maximum running speed of 50 km/h, while other studies based on shin bone strength estimated a speed of 14 m/s.
It possessed large, curved, and laterally thin toe claws that were likely used to stab prey, similar to modern predatory birds.
Studies of ear anatomy reveal that Patagornis had poor hearing with the smallest hearing range among the Cariamiformes examined.
Due to its body mass, the animal likely exhibited sluggish head movements but had enhanced sensitivity to low-amplitude motions.
The first Patagornis fossils were discovered by Museo de La Plata crews in the late 1880s.
John Bell Hatcher led Princeton University expeditions to Santa Cruz Province between 1896 and 1899.
The genus Patagornis was described by Francisco Moreno and Alcides Mercerat in 1891, with the species first named Patagornis marshi in May of that year.
Florentino Ameghino described the genus Tolmodus in August 1891 based on a premaxilla fragment.
Patagornis likely preyed on small to medium-sized mammals including the litoptern Thoatherium and the ground sloth Hapalops.
It may have competed with carnivorous sparassodont marsupials like Arctodictis and Prothylacinus for food.
The leg bone ratio in Patagornis suggests it was a very agile animal, as the tarsometatarsus is approximately 70% the length of the tibiotarsus.
Theories suggest Patagornis used its elongate feathers either to assist in running or as a defensive shield similar to the secretarybird.
Scientists suggest Patagornis likely used its strong legs to break the bones of medium-sized mammals rather than for high-speed running.
Bone histology suggests Patagornis reached sexual and skeletal maturity before achieving full somatic maturity.
Fossils show a smooth outer bone texture, indicating the specimens were fully grown individuals.
Patagornis is often considered the type genus of the subfamily Patagornithinae.
Mercerat established the family Patagornithidae in 1897 to group Patagornis and Pelecyornis based on shared features of their humeri and tarsometatarsi.
According to the principle of priority, the valid name is Patagornis marshi because it was described a month before the alternative name, and the genus authority is Moreno & Mercerat (1891).
Patagornis lived during the Early to Middle Miocene epochs.
The Santa Cruz Formation, where Patagornis fossils were found, dates from approximately 17.5 to 11.6 million years ago.
The initial Patagornis fossils were originally thought to be from the Eocene but are now dated to the upper Middle Miocene.
Remains are known mostly from outcrops of the Santa Cruz Formation along the Atlantic coast of southern Argentina.

Some scientists continue to use the name Tolmodus instead of Patagornis despite Patagornis marshi being the correct name under ICZN rules, while a few researchers still prefer the name Tolmodus inflatus.
A 2012 study suggested phorusrhacids could not hunt prey larger than themselves, but later studies countered this by noting extant birds can hunt significantly larger prey.
